{{Short description|Theorem in group theory}}
In [[group theory]], '''Schreier's lemma''' is a [[theorem]] used in the [[Schreier–Sims algorithm]] and also for finding a [[presentation of a group|presentation]] of a [[subgroup]].

== Statement ==
Suppose <math>H</math> is a subgroup of <math>G</math> with [[Generating set of a group|generating set]] <math>S</math>, that is, <math>G = \langle S\rangle</math>.

Let <math>R</math> be a right [[Transversal (combinatorics)|transversal]] of <math>H</math> in <math>G</math> with the neutral element <math>e</math> in <math>R</math>. In other words, let <math>R</math> be a set containing exactly one element from each right [[coset]] of <math>H</math> in <math>G</math>.

For each <math>g\in G</math>, we define <math>\overline{g}</math> as the chosen representative of the coset <math>Hg</math> in the transversal <math>R</math>.

Then <math>H</math> is generated by the set
:<math>\{rs(\overline{rs})^{-1}|r\in R, s\in S\}</math>.<ref name= Seress >{{cite book |last=Seress |first=Ákos |year=2002 |title=Permutation group algorithms |series=Cambridge Tracts in Mathematics |volume=152 |location=New York |publisher=Cambridge University Press |chapter=Bases and Strong Generating Sets, §4.2 The Schreier—Sims Algorithm |page=57}}</ref><ref name= Johnson >{{cite book |last=Johnson |first=David Lawrence |year=1980 |title=Topics in the Theory of Group Presentations |series=London Mathematical Society Lecture Note Series |volume=42 |location=New York |publisher=Cambridge University Press |chapter=Free groups and free presentations, §2 The Nielsen–Schreier theorem |page=13, Lemma 3}}</ref>

Hence, in particular, Schreier's lemma implies that every subgroup of finite [[Index of a subgroup|index]] of a finitely generated group is again finitely generated.<ref name= Holt >{{citation
|last      = Holt
|first     = Derek
|date      = April 2013
|title     = Presentation of Groups (Notes by F. Bouyer)
|publisher = The University of Warwick
|url       = https://warwick.ac.uk/fac/sci/maths/people/staff/fbouyer/presentation_of_group.pdf
|page      = 8, Corollary 3.8
}}&emsp; Erratum: "|Z| {{font|text==|color=red}} |X|·|U|" should read "|Z| {{font|text=≤|color=green}} |X|·|U|"</ref>

== Example ==
The group <math>\mathbb{Z}_3 = \mathbb{Z}\,/\,3 \mathbb{Z}</math> is cyclic. Via [[Cayley's theorem]], <math>\mathbb{Z}_3</math> is isomorphic to a subgroup of the [[symmetric group]] <math>S_3</math>. Now,
: <math>\mathbb{Z}_3 = \{ e, (1\ 2\ 3), (1\ 3\ 2) \}</math>
: <math>S_3 = \{ e, (1\ 2), (1\ 3), (2\ 3), (1\ 2\ 3), (1\ 3\ 2) \}</math>
where <math>e</math> is the identity [[permutation]]. Note that <math>S_3</math> is generated by <math>S = \{ s_1 = (1\ 2),\, s_2 = (1\ 2\ 3) \}</math>.

<math>\mathbb{Z}_3</math> has just two right cosets in <math>S_3</math>, namely <math>\mathbb{Z}_3</math> and <math>S_3 \setminus \mathbb{Z}_3 = \{ (1\ 2), (1\ 3), (2\ 3)\}</math>, so we select the right transversal <math>R = \{ r_1 = e,\, r_2 = (1\ 2) \}</math>, and we have
: <math>\begin{align}
r_1s_1 &= (1\ 2),    & \text{so} && \overline{r_1s_1} &= (1\ 2) \\
r_1s_2 &= (1\ 2\ 3), & \text{so} && \overline{r_1s_2} &= e \\
r_2s_1 &= e ,        & \text{so} && \overline{r_2s_1} &= e \\
r_2s_2 &= (2\ 3),    & \text{so} && \overline{r_2s_2} &= (1\ 2). \\
\end{align}</math>

Finally,
: <math>r_1s_1\left(\overline{r_1s_1}\right)^{-1} = e</math>
: <math>r_1s_2\left(\overline{r_1s_2}\right)^{-1} = (1\ 2\ 3)</math>
: <math>r_2s_1\left(\overline{r_2s_1}\right)^{-1} = e</math>
: <math>r_2s_2\left(\overline{r_2s_2}\right)^{-1} = (1\ 2\ 3).</math>

Thus, by Schreier's lemma, <math>\{ e, (1\ 2\ 3) \}</math> generates <math>\mathbb{Z}_3</math>, but having the identity in the generating set is redundant, so it can be removed to obtain another generating set for <math>\mathbb{Z}_3</math>, <math>\{ (1\ 2\ 3) \}</math>.
